concepts.name: Turtle Programming
concepts.summary: Turtle programming lets you give commands to a virtual turtle, telling it where to move on the screen. It is like having a small robot artist you can control with code, using a pre-installed Python tool called the turtle module.
key_points: The turtle module comes pre-installed with Python
You can tell the turtle to move forward, turn left or right, and change the line color
Turtle commands let you draw pictures on the screen
concepts.example_code: We'll start by learning turtle programming, which lets you give commands to a virtual turtle.

concepts.name: Coding Environment
concepts.summary: Before you can start drawing, you set up a coding environment such as Visual Studio Code, GitHub Codespaces, or the League Code Server. This is where you read lessons and run your programs.
key_points: You can use Visual Studio Code, GitHub Codespaces, or the League Code Server
You open a Codespace by clicking a button like 'Create codespace on master'
The setup is done before you start drawing
concepts.example_code: Create codespace on master

concepts.name: Virtual Screen
concepts.summary: To see your turtle's drawings, you open a virtual screen. It usually opens automatically, but if it does not you can click the little monitor icon in the top right corner of the editor, then click the connect button.
key_points: The virtual screen is where your turtle's drawings appear
It usually opens automatically
If it does not appear, click the monitor icon in the top right corner, then click connect
concepts.example_code: click the little monitor icon in the top right corner of your editor

concepts.name: Notebook and Python Files
concepts.summary: You can run Python in two main ways. Notebook files end with .ipynb and let you read text and run code in the same document. Python files end with .py and run as standalone programs.
key_points: Notebook files end with .ipynb
Python files end with .py
Notebooks let you combine readable text and runnable code in one document
concepts.example_code: .ipynb

concepts.name: Code Cells
concepts.summary: In a notebook, a code cell is a box where you can write and run code. You run a cell by clicking the play button or by pressing Shift + Enter.
key_points: A code cell is a box where you write and run code
Run a cell with the play button or Shift + Enter
Run All runs every code cell from top to bottom
concepts.example_code: Shift + Enter

concepts.name: Choosing the Python Interpreter
concepts.summary: The first time you press the play button, nothing visible may happen because you still need to pick which interpreter (version) of Python to use. You choose one from a dropdown, looking for an option with a star or .venv in the name.
key_points: You must pick a Python interpreter before code will run
Look for an option with a star or .venv in the name
You need to pick an interpreter each time you open a new notebook
concepts.example_code: Now click on a Python option from the list (look for one with a star or .venv in the name)

concepts.name: Running Code and print
concepts.summary: The first code you run prints text to the screen. The print command displays text, and a string is text written inside quotation marks. Your first assignment is to print Hello World and your name.
key_points: print displays text on the screen
Text inside quotation marks is a string
Changing the text inside the quotes changes what is printed
concepts.example_code: print("Hello World!")

concepts.name: Closing a Turtle Window
concepts.summary: When a turtle program finishes, you close its window to stop it. If the program ends with turtle.exitonclick(), you can simply click anywhere inside the window to close it.
key_points: Close a running program before starting another
You can click the X in the top-right corner to close a window
If the code ends with turtle.exitonclick(), clicking inside the window closes it
concepts.example_code: turtle.exitonclick()

concepts.name: Importing turtle and Creating a Turtle
concepts.summary: Most turtle programs start by importing the turtle module, setting up a window, and creating a turtle object. The turtle is given a name like tina so you can send it commands.
key_points: import turtle tells Python you want to work with the turtle module
turtle.setup(600, 600, 0, 0) sets the size of the window
tina = turtle.Turtle() creates a turtle named tina
concepts.example_code:
import turtle
turtle.setup(600, 600, 0, 0)
tina = turtle.Turtle()

concepts.name: Commands and Comments
concepts.summary: The code before the # is a command, an instruction that tells Tina what to do. The text after the # is a comment, a note for humans that Python ignores when it runs the program.
key_points: A command is an instruction that tells the turtle what to do
A comment starts with # and explains the code to humans
Comments are ignored by Python and do not affect how the program runs
concepts.example_code: tina.forward(200)                       # Move tina forward by 200 steps

concepts.name: Moving and Turning Tina
concepts.summary: You move Tina with forward and turn her with right or left. forward takes a number of steps, and right and left take an angle in degrees.
key_points: tina.forward(200) moves Tina forward 200 steps
tina.right(90) turns Tina right 90 degrees
Movement and turning commands take a number inside the parentheses
concepts.example_code:
tina.forward(200)
tina.right(90)

concepts.name: Pen Up and Pen Down
concepts.summary: penup lifts the pen so Tina can move without drawing, and pendown puts the pen back down so she draws again. You use these to reposition the turtle without leaving a line.
key_points: tina.penup() lifts the pen so Tina moves without drawing
tina.pendown() puts the pen down so Tina draws again
Use penup and pendown to move to a new spot without a line
concepts.example_code:
tina.penup()
tina.goto(-100, 100)
tina.pendown()

concepts.name: Moving to a Position with goto
concepts.summary: goto moves the turtle directly to a position given by an x and y coordinate. It is often used with penup so you can reposition without drawing.
key_points: tina.goto(-100, 100) moves Tina to the x, y position (-100, 100)
goto takes two numbers: the x coordinate and the y coordinate
goto is often paired with penup to move without drawing
concepts.example_code: tina.goto(-100, 100)

concepts.name: Pen Color
concepts.summary: pencolor changes the color of the line Tina draws. You pass the color name as a string, such as 'blue' or 'red'.
key_points: tina.pencolor('blue') sets the pen color to blue
The color name is written as a string in quotes
Changing the pen color before drawing makes lines different colors
concepts.example_code: tina.pencolor('blue')                   # Set the pen color to blue

concepts.name: Turtle Shape and Speed
concepts.summary: shape sets what the turtle looks like, and speed controls how fast it moves. A speed of 2 is moderate, while 'fastest' draws as quickly as possible.
key_points: tina.shape('turtle') makes the cursor look like a turtle
tina.speed(2) moves at a moderate speed
tina.speed('fastest') draws as quickly as possible
concepts.example_code:
tina.shape('turtle')
tina.speed(2)

concepts.name: Drawing and Filling a Circle
concepts.summary: circle draws a circle with the given radius. To fill a shape with color you call begin_fill before drawing and end_fill after, and color sets the fill color.
key_points: tina.circle(75) draws a circle with radius 75
begin_fill() and end_fill() surround a shape to fill it with color
tina.color('red') sets the color used for the fill
concepts.example_code:
tina.color('red')
tina.begin_fill()
tina.circle(75)
tina.end_fill()

concepts.name: Writing Text
concepts.summary: write displays text on the screen at the turtle's current position. You pass the message as a string inside the parentheses.
key_points: tina.write("Why, hello there!") writes a message on the screen
The text goes inside quotation marks
Text appears at the turtle's current position
concepts.example_code: tina.write("Why, hello there!")

concepts.name: Docstrings
concepts.summary: Text enclosed in triple quotes at the top of a file is a docstring, which gives a multi-line explanation of what the program does. It is different from a single-line # comment.
key_points: A docstring is text enclosed in triple quotes
Docstrings provide a multi-line explanation, often at the top of a file
Single-line comments start with #
concepts.example_code:
"""
# Squares_and_Circles.py
...
"""

concepts.name: Checking In Your Code
concepts.summary: Checking in your code means saving your progress to a Source Control System like Git, so your work is safely stored and can be restored later. You commit your changes with a message and then sync them to GitHub.
key_points: Checking in uses a Source Control System like Git
You enter a commit message, click Commit, then Sync to upload to GitHub
Commit often so you do not lose work
concepts.example_code: Enter a message in the Message box describing what you changed.

concepts.name: Using Documentation
concepts.summary: Reading documentation helps you find commands, learn features, and fix errors on your own. The official Python Turtle documentation lists every command you can use.
key_points: Documentation helps you learn correct syntax and discover features
The official Turtle documentation lists every command
Copying example code and changing it is a good way to learn
concepts.example_code: python turtle commands

concepts.name: The Standard Turtle Program Setup
concepts.summary: Most turtle programs begin with the same three lines: import the turtle module, set up the window, and create a turtle named tina. These lines are needed in nearly every turtle program.
key_points: import turtle loads the turtle module
turtle.setup(600, 600, 0, 0) sets the size of the window
tina = turtle.Turtle() creates the turtle you give commands to
concepts.example_code:
import turtle
turtle.setup(600, 600, 0, 0)
tina = turtle.Turtle()

concepts.name: Drawing a Triangle
concepts.summary: You draw an equilateral triangle by moving Tina forward and turning her left to make each of the three sides. Changing the pen color before each side makes each side a different color.
key_points: Use tina.forward() and tina.left() to draw the three sides
Change the color with tina.pencolor() before each side
An equilateral triangle has three equal sides
concepts.example_code: # Use tina.forward() and tina.left() to draw a triangle

concepts.name: Drawing a Pentagon
concepts.summary: A pentagon is a five-sided shape. You draw it using forward, left, and pencolor commands, making each of the five sides a different color.
key_points: A pentagon has five sides
Use tina.forward(), tina.left(), and tina.pencolor()
Each side can be a different color
concepts.example_code: # Use tina.forward() and tina.left() to draw a pentagon

concepts.name: Drawing Multiple Filled Shapes
concepts.summary: You can draw several shapes by moving the turtle to a new spot with goto between them. To fill each shape with its own color you use begin_fill, fillcolor, circle, and end_fill.
key_points: Use tina.goto() to move to a new spot for each shape
Use begin_fill(), fillcolor(), and end_fill() to fill a shape
Shapes should be positioned so they do not overlap
concepts.example_code: # Use tina.begin_fill(), tina.end_fill(), and tina.fillcolor() to fill in the shapes

concepts.name: Exercise Placeholders
concepts.summary: These exercise files leave a placeholder where you write your own code, marked by '... # Your code here'. You fill in the missing commands between the setup lines and turtle.exitonclick().
key_points: '... # Your code here' marks where you write your own code
The setup lines and turtle.exitonclick() are already provided
You refer to earlier programs like Meet_Tina.py for examples
concepts.example_code: ... # Your code here

concepts.name: Why Use Loops
concepts.summary: Loops let you run the same code many times without repeating yourself. They save time, reduce mistakes, and make updates easier because changing one line in a loop applies everywhere.
key_points: Loops run the same code many times without repeating lines
They save time and reduce mistakes from repeated lines
Changing one part of a loop applies the change everywhere it runs
concepts.example_code: Loops let you run the same code many times without repeating yourself.

concepts.name: for Loops and range
concepts.summary: A for loop repeats the indented lines a set number of times. range(4) generates the numbers 0, 1, 2, 3, so the loop runs four times, and the variable i takes each value in turn.
key_points: for i in range(4): runs the indented code four times
range(4) generates the numbers 0, 1, 2, 3
The variable i takes each value in the range, one per iteration
concepts.example_code:
for i in range(4):                          # Loop will run 4 times from 0 to 3
    print('Loop Iteration', i)

concepts.name: Indentation in Loops
concepts.summary: The lines that run inside a for loop are indented under the for statement. Only the indented lines are repeated each time the loop runs.
key_points: Indented lines under for are the body that repeats
Indentation tells Python which lines belong to the loop
Lines that are not indented are not part of the loop

concepts.name: Drawing Shapes with Loops
concepts.summary: Repeating a forward and a turn inside a loop draws a polygon. The number of repeats is the number of sides, and the turn angle changes for each shape.
key_points: A square repeats forward and left 4 times turning 90 degrees
A triangle repeats forward and left 3 times turning 120 degrees
To draw a hexagon you change range(4) to range(6) and the angle from 90 to 60
concepts.example_code:
for i in range(4):                          # Loop 4 times
    tina.forward(100)                       # Move forward 100 units
    tina.left(90)                           # Turn left 90 degrees

concepts.name: Nested Loops
concepts.summary: A nested loop is a loop inside another loop. The outer loop handles the rows and the inner loop handles the columns, which is useful for making grid patterns like a checkerboard.
key_points: A nested loop is a loop placed inside another loop
The outer loop handles rows, the inner loop handles columns
Nested loops are good for grid patterns

concepts.name: Repeating a String with *
concepts.summary: Multiplying a string by a number repeats it that many times. For example, '🟧' * size prints a row of that many orange squares.
key_points: Multiplying a string by a number repeats the string
'🟧' * size makes a row of size orange squares
This is used inside a loop to print rows
concepts.example_code: print('🟧' * size)

concepts.name: print with end
concepts.summary: Normally print moves to a new line, but print('x', end='') keeps printing on the same line. A plain print() at the end of an inner loop moves to the next line to start a new row.
key_points: print('⚫️', end='') keeps output on the same line
A plain print() moves to the next line
Using end='' and print() together builds rows in a grid
concepts.example_code: print('⚫️', end='')

concepts.name: Loop Exercises with Turtle
concepts.summary: The exercises ask you to replace repeated movement lines with a for loop that runs the right number of times. For a square the loop runs four times; for a pentagon it runs five times.
key_points: Replace repeated forward and left lines with a for loop
A square needs a loop that runs four times
A regular pentagon needs a loop that runs five times
concepts.example_code: Replace the repeated movement and turning lines with a for loop that runs four times.

concepts.name: What Is a Variable
concepts.summary: A variable is like a labeled box that stores information such as numbers or words. You can change what is inside anytime, and the program uses the value when it runs.
key_points: A variable is a name that holds a value
You store a value with the form name = value, like sides = 6
Using a variable lets you change a value in one place
concepts.example_code: sides = 6

concepts.name: Types of Variables
concepts.summary: Variables can store different types of data. An integer is a whole number, a float is a number with a decimal point, a string is text in quotes, and a boolean is either True or False.
key_points: An integer is a whole number like 12
A float is a number with a decimal point like 98.6
A boolean can only be True or False
concepts.example_code:
my_age = 12                                 # This is an integer (a whole number)
temperature = 98.6                          # This is a float (a fractional number)
is_sunny = True

concepts.name: Calculating with Variables
concepts.summary: Variables let you do calculations, and a calculated variable updates automatically when its inputs change. The angle for a regular polygon is found with angle = 360 / sides.
key_points: A variable can be calculated from other variables
angle = 360 / sides gives the turn angle for a regular polygon
If you change sides, angle updates automatically
concepts.example_code: angle = 360 / sides

concepts.name: Variables in Loops
concepts.summary: A loop variable like sides can take a range of values, letting you repeat a calculation for each one. Using a variable for the number of sides lets Tina draw any polygon by changing one number.
key_points: for sides in range(1, 10): loops sides through 1 to 9
The calculation inside the loop uses the current value of sides
Variables let Tina draw any polygon by changing one number

concepts.name: What Is a Function
concepts.summary: A function is a named block of code that does a specific job. You can call it whenever you need it instead of writing the same code over and over, which helps you organize and reuse code.
key_points: A function is a named block of code that performs a task
You define a function with the word def followed by its name
Functions let you reuse code instead of copying it

concepts.name: Parameters and Arguments
concepts.summary: A parameter is a variable listed in the function definition that receives a value. An argument is the actual value you pass in when you call the function.
key_points: Parameters are listed inside the parentheses in the def line
Arguments are the values you pass when calling the function
Calling calculate_angle(4) sets the parameter sides to 4

concepts.name: Returning Values
concepts.summary: The return statement sends a value back to whoever called the function so it can be used elsewhere. A function can even return more than one value at once.
key_points: return sends a value back to the caller
You can store a returned value in a variable
A function can return more than one value using a comma

concepts.name: Functions with Tina
concepts.summary: You can write a function that draws a polygon for any number of sides, size, and color. Calling it with different arguments draws different shapes without repeating the drawing code.
key_points: def draw_polygon(sides, size, color="black") draws any polygon
The angle is calculated as 360 / sides inside the function
Calling the function with different arguments draws different shapes

concepts.name: Custom GIF Turtle Shapes
concepts.summary: You can change how the turtle looks by using your own image as its shape. The image must be a GIF, and you register it with the screen before setting it as the turtle's shape.
key_points: The image used for a turtle shape must be a GIF file.
First register the image with screen.addshape(path), then set it with turtle.shape(path).
Images are usually kept in an 'images' folder next to the program file.
concepts.example_code:
screen = turtle.getscreen()
screen.addshape(image_path)
turtle.shape(image_path)

concepts.name: Setting a Background Picture
concepts.summary: You can put an image behind the turtle as the window background using bgpic(). It accepts a GIF or PNG file stored in the images folder next to your program.
key_points: Use window.bgpic(image_path) to set a background image.
The background can be a GIF or a PNG.
You can size the window to match the image dimensions before setting the background.
concepts.example_code:
window.setup(image.width, image.height, startx=0, starty=0)
window.bgpic(image_path)

concepts.name: Multiple Turtles
concepts.summary: You can create more than one turtle on the same screen and move each one independently. Each turtle is its own object with its own pen, shape, and position.
key_points: Each call to turtle.Turtle() makes a separate turtle you can control on its own.
Different turtles can have different shapes, like 'turtle' and 'arrow'.
Inside a loop you can move every turtle to its own position each step.
concepts.example_code:
t1 = turtle.Turtle()
t2 = turtle.Turtle()
for i in range(-200, 200):
    t1.goto(i, i)
    t2.goto(i, -i)

concepts.name: Moving With goto and Coordinates
concepts.summary: The goto(x, y) command moves a turtle straight to a point given by its x and y coordinates. Lifting the pen first lets the turtle move without drawing.
key_points: goto(x, y) sends the turtle to that exact point on the screen.
The center of the screen is (0, 0); x grows to the right and y grows upward.
Use penup() before goto if you don't want a line drawn while moving.

concepts.name: Responding to Screen Clicks
concepts.summary: You can make a program react when the user clicks anywhere on the screen by passing a function to screen.onclick(). The function receives the x and y coordinates of the click.
key_points: screen.onclick(function) connects a function to screen clicks.
The click handler function is given the x and y coordinates as arguments.
Use turtle.done() (not exitonclick) to keep the window open so clicks still register.
concepts.example_code:
def screen_clicked(x, y):
    print('You pressed: x=' + str(x) + ', y=' + str(y))
    t.goto(x, y)

screen.onclick(screen_clicked)

concepts.name: Clicking a Turtle With a Lambda
concepts.summary: You can run a function when the user clicks a specific turtle using t.onclick(). A lambda is used so the handler also knows which turtle was clicked, not just the x and y.
key_points: t.onclick(...) runs a function when that particular turtle is clicked.
A lambda lets you pass the turtle along with the x and y coordinates.
The t=t part locks in the current turtle so the handler doesn't mix up turtles.
concepts.example_code: t.onclick(lambda x, y, t=t: turtle_clicked(t, x, y))

concepts.name: What a List Is
concepts.summary: A list is a built-in Python data structure that stores an ordered collection of items. You write a list using square brackets with the items separated by commas.
key_points: A list holds an ordered collection of items.
Lists are written with square brackets, like ['apples', 'oranges'].
Items in a list are separated by commas.
concepts.example_code: things_to_buy = ['apples', 'oranges', 'bread', 'milk']

concepts.name: Indexing a List
concepts.summary: You can get a single item from a list using square brackets and a number called an index. Indexes start at 0, so the first item is at index 0 and the second item is at index 1.
key_points: Indexing uses square brackets with a number, like things_to_buy[1].
Indexes start at 0, so the first item is at index 0.
things_to_buy[1] gets the second item.
concepts.example_code:
things_to_buy = ['apples', 'oranges', 'bread', 'milk']
things_to_buy[1] # This gets the second item (index 1)

concepts.name: Iterating Over a List
concepts.summary: You can loop over a list with a for loop to do something with each item in turn. This is called iteration and is very common in programs.
key_points: A for loop goes through a list one item at a time.
The loop variable holds the current item each time through.
Looping over a list of items lets you act on each one.
concepts.example_code:
for item in things_to_buy:
    print(item)

concepts.name: Common List Operations
concepts.summary: Lists support handy operations: append adds to the end, insert adds at a position, remove deletes an item, len counts the items, and slicing returns a sub-list.
key_points: append(x) adds x to the end of the list.
insert(i, x) inserts x at index i; remove(x) deletes the first matching item.
len(list) gives the number of items, and list[start:stop] returns a sub-list (slicing).
concepts.example_code:
items.append('cherry')
items.insert(1, 'orange')
items.remove('banana')
print('Length:', len(items))
print('Slice (0:2):', items[0:2])

concepts.name: Looping a List of Colors With the Turtle
concepts.summary: You can store colors in a list and loop over them so the turtle uses a different color for each side it draws. This combines lists with turtle drawing.
key_points: Storing colors in a list lets you reuse them in a loop.
Each pass of the loop sets one color and draws one side.
You can loop over a list of values to control turtle actions like color or angle.
concepts.example_code:
colors = [ 'red', 'blue', 'black', 'orange']
for color in colors:
    tina.color(color)
    tina.forward(forward)
    tina.left(left)

concepts.name: Data Types
concepts.summary: Every value in Python has a type, like integer, float, string, or list. The type decides what operations you can do with the value.
key_points: Integers are whole numbers like 3; floats have a decimal part like 3.5.
Strings are text like "Alice"; lists are ordered sequences like ['red', 'blue'].
Strings are immutable (can't be changed); lists are mutable (can be changed).
concepts.example_code:
age = 14
bank_account = 159.99
name = "John"
colors = ["red", "blue", "green"]

concepts.name: The type() Function
concepts.summary: The type() function tells you what kind of value a variable holds. This helps you know which operations are allowed.
key_points: type(x) returns the data type of x.
Knowing a value's type tells you how it behaves when combined with other values.
concepts.example_code:
print("Age    : ", type(age))
print("Name   : ", type(name))

concepts.name: Addition vs Concatenation
concepts.summary: The + operator adds numbers together, but with strings it joins (concatenates) them end to end. The result depends on the type of the values.
key_points: 10 + 20 with integers gives 30.
"10" + "20" with strings gives "1020".
Joining strings together is called concatenation.
concepts.example_code:
x = "10"
y = "20"
print("x + y =", x + y) # Watch what happens.

concepts.name: TypeError and Type Conversion
concepts.summary: You can't add an integer to a string directly; it raises a TypeError. You first convert one value with int() or str() so both are the same type.
key_points: Adding an int and a str directly causes a TypeError.
int() turns a string into an integer; str() turns a number into a string.
The conversion function has the same name as the type you want to make.
concepts.example_code:
x = 10
y = "20"
print("Integer:", x + int(y))
print("String:", str(x) + y)

concepts.name: Math Operators
concepts.summary: Python has operators for arithmetic: + - * / for the basics, plus // for floor division, % for remainder, and ** for powers.
key_points: / is regular division and always gives a float.
** is exponentiation, so 2 ** 3 is 8.
* is multiplication and - is subtraction.
concepts.example_code: print(22 / 7)

concepts.name: Floor Division
concepts.summary: Floor division (//) divides and throws away anything after the decimal point. With integers you get an integer; with floats you get a float.
key_points: 11 // 4 gives 2 because 4 goes into 11 two whole times.
Integer // integer gives an integer; float // float gives a float.
Regular division (/) always gives a float, even with integers.

concepts.name: Modulo Operator
concepts.summary: The modulo operator (%) gives the remainder after dividing one number by another. It is often used to check whether a number is even or odd.
key_points: 4 % 2 == 0 means 4 is even (no remainder).
5 % 2 == 1 means 5 is odd.
If n % divisor == 0, then n is evenly divisible by that divisor.

concepts.name: Connecting Division and Modulo
concepts.summary: Floor division gives the quotient and modulo gives the remainder. Together they break a number into two parts you can use to rebuild the original.
key_points: quotient = dividend // divisor.
remainder = dividend % divisor.
dividend = (quotient * divisor) + remainder.
concepts.example_code:
dividend = 11
divisor = 4
quotient = dividend // divisor
remainder = dividend % divisor

concepts.name: Creating Strings
concepts.summary: Strings are sequences of characters used for text. You create them by wrapping text in single quotes '...' or double quotes "...".
key_points: Single and double quotes both work for strings.
Strings are immutable, so they can't be changed after creation.
Strings can't be used in math operations without conversion.
concepts.example_code:
a = 'Hello' # Define with single quotes
b = "World" # Define with double quotes

concepts.name: Concatenation and Repetition
concepts.summary: The + operator joins strings together, and the * operator repeats a string a given number of times.
key_points: + concatenates two strings into one.
* repeats a string, so 'Hello' * 3 makes 'HelloHelloHello'.
These operators look like math but work on text.
concepts.example_code:
print(a + " " + b + '!')
print(a * 3)

concepts.name: Indexing
concepts.summary: Indexing uses square brackets to grab a single character from a string. Counting starts at 0, and negative indices count from the end.
key_points: a[0] is the first character.
a[-1] is the last character.
Indexing returns one character.
concepts.example_code:
print(a[0]) # Indexing, get the first letter
print(a[-1]) # Indexing, get the last letter

concepts.name: Slicing Strings
concepts.summary: Slicing extracts part of a string with string[start:end]. The start index is included and the end index is not.
key_points: text[0:6] gives characters from index 0 up to but not including 6.
text[7:] goes from index 7 to the end.
text[-11:] takes the last 11 characters.
The end index is not included in the slice.
concepts.example_code:
text = "Python Programming"
print(text[0:6])
print(text[7:])

concepts.name: Length and Membership
concepts.summary: len() counts the characters in a string. The in and not in operators check whether one string appears inside another, returning True or False.
key_points: len(s) returns the number of characters.
"secret" in password is True if the substring exists.
not in returns True when the substring is absent.
concepts.example_code:
print("Length:", len(password))
print("Contains 'secret':", "secret" in password)

concepts.name: String Methods
concepts.summary: Strings have built-in methods like .upper(), .lower(), .title(), .replace(), and .split(). Because strings are immutable, these methods return a new string instead of changing the original.
key_points: .upper() and .lower() change case; .title() capitalizes each word.
.replace(old, new) swaps text; .split() breaks a string at spaces into a list.
.strip() removes leading and trailing spaces.
String methods return a new string, not a changed one.
concepts.example_code:
s = "Hello World!"
print(s.upper())
print(s.replace('World', 'Python'))
print(s.split())

concepts.name: Escape Characters
concepts.summary: A backslash lets you include special characters in a string, such as a newline (\n), a tab (\t), or a quote (\").
key_points: \n starts a new line.
\t inserts a tab.
\" and \' print quotes; \\ prints a backslash.
concepts.example_code:
print("Line 1\nLine 2")
print("She said, \"Hello!\"")

concepts.name: f-strings
concepts.summary: An f-string is a string with an f before the opening quote that lets you embed variables and expressions inside curly braces {}.
key_points: Put f before the quote to make an f-string.
Variables go inside curly braces, like {name}.
You can do math inside the braces, like {score + 5}.
concepts.example_code:
message = f"Player {name} scored {score} points."
print(f"Next level requires {score + 5} points.")

concepts.name: if Statements
concepts.summary: An if statement runs a block of indented code only when its condition is True. This lets a program make decisions, also called control flow or branching.
key_points: The code after if runs only if the condition evaluates to True.
The conditional code must be indented under the if.

concepts.name: Parts of a Function
concepts.summary: A function has a name (after def), parameters (the inputs in parentheses), a body (the indented code), and a return value (its output). If a function has no return statement, it returns None.
key_points: The name comes right after def.
Parameters are the inputs listed in parentheses.
The body is the indented block that runs when the function is called.
A function with no return statement returns None.

concepts.name: pass and None

concepts.name: Positional and Keyword Arguments
concepts.summary: When calling a function you can pass values positionally (in order) or by name using keywords (in any order). You can mix them, but positional arguments must come before keyword arguments.
key_points: Positional arguments match parameters in order.
Keyword arguments are passed by name and can be in any order.
When mixing, positional arguments must come first.
You cannot put a positional argument after a keyword argument.

    print(f"{greeting}, {name}!")

greet_user("Alice", "Bonjour")

greet_user("Bob", greeting="Hello")

concepts.name: Default Arguments
concepts.summary: You can give a parameter a default value so it becomes optional when calling the function. Parameters with defaults must come after parameters without defaults.
key_points: A default value is written with = in the parameter list.
If you do not pass a value, the default is used.
Parameters with defaults must come after parameters without defaults.

concepts.name: What an Exception Is
